items.title: What is WRF-Chem-Polar?
items.text: WRF-Chem-Polar is a regional chemistry-climate model based on WRF-Chem, with enhancements for the polar regions, developed at IGE and LATMOS in France. We develop scientific code for the model itself and also a variety of tools for each step of the modelling process.

items.title: Our repositories
items.text:
• The WRF-Chem-Polar model code.
  • WRF-infra: all you need to run and compile the model.
  • The wrfpp Python package to post-process WRF outputs.

items.title: Compiling WRF and related tools
items.text:
Warning

It is quite likely that the installation process described below will not work if you are working in an environment where conda is activated. We therefore recommand to

  • not automatically activate a conda environment in your ~/.bashrc file
  • deactivate any activated conda environment, if any, before proceeding further

items.title: Basic usage
items.text:
Use the compile_WRF.py script provided in WRF-infra to download and compile WRF:

cd WRF-infra/compile
python compile_WRF.py

This compiles WRF-Chem-Polar with chemistry activated. Compilation takes roughly an hour and a half. You can check that compilation was successful by looking for the following message at the end of compilation.log in your installation directory:

--->                  Executables successfully built                  <---

The default configuration of this script is based on the WRF-Chem-Polar team's most frequent use-case. Subsections below explain how to use different settings (see also this technical documentation for a description of all the existing options).

items.title: Compile upstream WRF
items.text:
Use the --upstream switch to compile the upstream version of WRF or WRF-Chem:

python compile_WRF.py --upstream

items.title: Compile WRF without WRF-Chem
items.text:
To use WRF in meteorology-only mode, tell the script not to compile any extra components:

python compile_WRF.py --components ""

(the default value of this parameter is "kpp,chem").

items.title: Choose where to install WRF
items.text:
By default, the script installs WRF in a directory named "WRF". Use the option --destination to install it to a directory of your choice, for instance:

python compile_WRF.py --destination=/path/to/my/wrf

items.title: Using a scheduler (or not)
items.text:
By default, the compile script sends all the work to the host's scheduler (eg. slurm). You can prevent this behaviour using:

python compile_WRF.py --scheduler no

On some machines, the scheduler requires that a project name be specified when running a job, which you can do using:

python compile_WRF.py --scheduler-opt account ${my-account-name}

More generally, you can set any scheduler option using the following syntax:

python compile_WRF.py --scheduler-opt ${option-name} ${option-value}

items.title: Compile WPS
items.text:
Although it is a pre-processor, WPS needs to be compiled after WRF because it depends on it. Use the compile_WPS.py script to download and compile the latest WPS version:

python compile_WPS.py

Compilation of WPS typically takes one or two minutes. You can verify that compilation was successful by checking for the presence of the following binaries in the installation directory (presence of the actual binaries in the */src directories and of the simlinks at the root of the directory):

  • geogrid.exe -> geogrid/src/geogrid.exe
  • metgrid.exe -> metgrid/src/metgrid.exe
  • ungrib.exe -> ungrib/src/ungrib.exe

Just as for WRF, you can use the parameter --destination to specify where WPS should be installed. Additionally, if you installed WRF in a non-default location, you will have to use the option --wrfdir to point to where WRF is installed, for example:

python compile_WPS.py --destination=/path/to/my/wps --wrfdir=/path/to/my/wrf

Note that patches are required to compile WPS v4.6.0:

python compile_WPS.py --commit v4.6.0 --patches ./patches/WPS/v4.6.0

items.title: Why WRF-infra?
items.text:
Running meaningful WRF or WRF-Chem simulations is not trivial. It involves many steps beyond just running the model. Running simulations that can be reproduced at a later time is even more challenging.

WRF-infra is a set of tools that aim to make the development and use of WRF and its derivatives:

  • easier
  • more transparent
  • more reproducible

WRF-infra facilitates many steps of the modelling process:

  • compiling WRF, WPS, and the WRF-Chem pre-processing tools
  • fetching input data from reliable sources
  • pre-processing said input data
  • running WPS
  • running the WRF and WRF-Chem models
  • testing new WRF and WRF-Chem developments

items.title: Getting WRF-infra
items.text:
Getting WRF-infra is just a matter of cloning the entire repository:

git clone https://github.com/WRF-Chem-Polar/WRF-infra.git

items.title: Setting up WRF-infra
items.text:
Basic WRF-infra functionality only requires Python 3.

Additional WRF-infra functionality (eg. some WRF pre-processors) may require additional dependencies. These are listed in pyproject.toml.

We recommend using mamba or micromamba to install these dependencies from conda-forge.

items.title: Support for multiple machines
items.text:
WRF-infra currently supports the following machines:

  • Dahu
  • Jean Zay
  • Jed
  • Spirit

A little bit of work is needed to use WRF and WRF-Chem on a new machine (eg. a new supercomputer).

WRF and WRF-Chem rely on external libraries such as NetCDF and flex. The availability and locations of such libraries may vary from one machine to the next. Additionally, you may want to use a scheduler such as slurm to compile and run WRF. Each machine may use a different scheduler. All these things must be sorted out before using WRF and WRF-Chem.

For simplicity, WRF-infra gathers up all the information needed for each machine it supports in so-called "environment files". There is one and only one environment file for each machine. This file defines both the compile-time and the run-time configuration for WRF and WRF-Chem. All environment files are located in the env directory of WRF-infra. The complete documentation for the syntax accepted by these files is here.

To add support for a new machine to WRF-infra, you "just" need to:

  1. Create the environment file for this machine in the env directory.
  2. Edit the file env/hosts to add the mapping between the machine's hostname and the file you just created.

items.title: The WRF-Chem-Polar model
items.text: WRF-Chem-Polar is a fork of NCAR's WRF model with enhancements for the polar regions. Most of WRF-Chem-Polar developments are available in the form of new namelist options. These are described here.

items.title: What is wrfpp?
items.text: wrfpp is a Python package that facilitates the analysis of WRF and WRF-Chem outputs.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
Tip

We strongly encourage you to work within some kind of isolated Python environment (eg. venv or conda)

You can install wrfpp and its dependencies with pip. It is recommended to install a tagged version (eg. "v1.0"):

pip install wrfpp[all]@git+https://github.com/WRF-Chem-Polar/wrfpp.git@v1.0

To install the latest development version, simply omit the tag:

pip install wrfpp[all]@git+https://github.com/WRF-Chem-Polar/wrfpp.git

You can choose not to install optional dependencies by omitting [all] in the commands above. Some features of wrfpp will not work in this case.

items.title: Versioning
items.text: For reproducible computing, please only use commits tagged with a version number (eg. "v2.3"). These uniquely and unequivocally define specific versions of wrfpp. This is not true for any version number that has the ".dev0" suffix (eg "v2.3.dev0").

items.title: Basic usage
items.text:
First open a WRF or WRF-Chem output file with wrfpp:

import wrfpp

ds = wrfpp.open_dataset("wrfout.nc")

wrfpp adds wrf-specific functionalities to xarray datasets via a tool called an accessor.

For all practical purposes, the ds object should behave exactly like any other xarray Dataset:

print(ds.variables)

items.title: Derived variables
items.text:
One of the main features of wrfpp is so-called derived variables. These are DataArray objects, just as any other dataset variable, but they are calculated on the fly by wrfpp instead of being read directly from the underlying WRF file.

For instance, WRF output files typically contain a variable T that is the potential air temperature relative to some reference value:

avg = ds.T.values.mean()
units = ds.T.units
print(f"Average relative potential temperature = {avg} {units}")

Average relative potential temperature = 43.795982360839844 K
However, air temperature is typically not found in WRF output files. Thanks to wrfpp's magic, we can use air_temperature as if it were a native variable:

avg = ds.air_temperature.values.mean()
units = ds.air_temperature.units
print(f"Average air temperature = {avg} {units}")

Average air temperature = 234.40847778320312 K

Thanks to this transparent syntax, one can write code that works agnostically on both native and derived WRF variables:

variables = ("T", "air_temperature", "QVAPOR", "relative_humidity")
for v in variables:
    data_array = getattr(ds, v)
    avg = data_array.values.mean()
    units = data_array.units
    print(f"{v}: {avg} {units}")

T: 43.795982360839844 K
air_temperature: 234.40847778320312 K
QVAPOR: 0.00043676584027707577 kg kg-1
relative_humidity: 31.046321868896484 %

The following table lists all derived variables available at this time:

Name Description grid_cell_area Grid cell area, accounting for projection deformation altitude_asl Grid cell altitude above sea level altitude_agl Grid cell altitude above ground level altitude_asl_c Grid cell centrepoint altitude above sea level altitude_agl_c Grid cell centrepoint altitude above ground level box_dz Grid box vertical extent potential_temperature Potential temperature atm_pressure Atmospheric pressure air_temperature Air temperature density_of_dry_air Dry air density relative_humidity Relative humidity accumulated_precipitation Accumulated total precipitation liquid_water_path Liquid water path cloud_liquid_water_path Cloud liquid water path ice_water_path Solid water path cloud_ice_water_path Cloud solid water path aer_number_conc_nonact Non-activated aerosol number concentration aer_number_conc_act Activated aerosol number concentration aer_number_conc_total Total aerosol number concentration fraction_activated_aerosol Number-based fraction of aerosols that are activated
